scene.speaker: nova
scene.bubble: Zoom out and look at the bigger picture — every repair, every recycled bottle and every choice about what we buy adds up. Let's see how English describes it all.
scene.intro: Welcome to Unit 4. The Inspiring Nordic project now zooms out from individual trades to the bigger picture: what happens to everything we make, use and throw away. In this unit you read an article, in the format of Reading and Use of English Part 5, about the throwaway culture and the people quietly fighting it. You learn relative clauses, the structures that let you add information smoothly without starting a new sentence, and quantifiers for talking about waste, energy and research. You listen to five speakers, in the format of Listening Part 3, describing what they personally do for the environment, and you write a report, in the format of Writing Part 2, about recycling at your school. Sofía, Mateo, Liam and Nadia have already started collecting ideas — let's join them and see the bigger picture.

activities.title: Speaking — Parts 1 and 2. Talk with a partner, then record yourself.

tips.expect: Part 1 (2 minutes): the examiner asks you and your partner questions about yourselves. Part 2 (about 4 minutes): each of you compares two of three photographs for about a minute, answering the question printed above them; then your partner answers a short question about your photos (about 20 seconds).
how: In Part 1, give a short reason or example, not one-word answers, but do not turn it into a speech.
In Part 2, do not simply describe the photographs. Compare them and answer both parts of the question: speculate (they might be…, perhaps she's hoping to…) and give your opinion.
Keep talking for the full minute. If you run out of things to say about the first question, move on to the second one.
tips.remember: You only need to talk about TWO of the three photographs — choose the two you can say most about.

data.text: Part 1: talk about shopping, waste and the environment. Part 2: compare two of the three photographs and say why the people might be doing this and what effect it might have on the environment.

activities.title: Reading and Use of English Part 5 — multiple choice. Read the article and choose the answer that fits best.

tips.expect: One text of about 500–650 words followed by six four-option questions. They test the main idea, detail, the writer's opinion or attitude, and simple inference. The questions follow the order of the text.
how: Read the whole text once, quickly, to get the general idea and the writer's attitude.
For each question, find the part of the text it refers to and read it closely. The correct option paraphrases the text; wrong options often reuse words from the text but change the meaning.
Do not choose an option just because it sounds true in general — check that it is what the writer actually says.
tips.remember: All four options usually relate to the right part of the text. Eliminate the ones that are almost right, not just obviously wrong.

data.title: The bigger picture
data.author: liam
data.text:
Have you ever wondered what actually happens to something after you throw it in the bin? Most of us never ask. We finish a drink, drop the bottle in, and move on with our day. Yet that single action is the start of a much longer journey — one that ends, more often than not, in a landfill site or a furnace. For our Inspiring Nordic project this term, we decided to follow that journey and see the bigger picture.

The numbers are hard to picture. Every year, the average person in a modern city throws away several hundred kilograms of rubbish — food, packaging, clothes, broken gadgets. Some of it can be recycled, but a surprising amount cannot, either because it is mixed with other materials or because nobody sorts it properly. What cannot be recycled is buried or burned, and both processes release gases that warm the planet. In other words, the bin in your kitchen is connected to something much bigger than your kitchen.

Part of the problem, our research suggested, is a habit rather than a single bad decision: the habit of replacing instead of repairing. A phone with a cracked screen, a jacket with a broken zip, a chair with a wobbly leg — these are usually thrown out rather than fixed, because a new one is often cheaper and always more convenient. Our grandparents' generation rarely had that choice. Clothes were mended, shoes were resoled, and furniture was passed down rather than thrown away. Somewhere along the way, that skill became rare.

This is where the trades we have been studying all term come back into the picture. Carpenters, tailors and electricians are, in a sense, the opposite of the throwaway culture: their entire job is to make things last longer. We visited a small repair workshop near school, whose owner spends her days bringing broken furniture back to life instead of sending it to landfill. “People are always surprised,” she told us, “that a chair somebody wanted to throw away can look brand new again.”

Of course, not every solution has to involve a workshop. Simple choices add up too: buying secondhand rather than new, choosing products with less packaging, or repairing a torn bag instead of replacing it. None of these choices is dramatic on its own, which is exactly why they are easy to forget. But multiply one small choice by a few million people, and the effect on landfill and emissions stops being small at all.

What struck us most, researching this article, was how disconnected the beginning and the end of an object's life usually feel. We rarely think about the landfill while we are shopping, and we rarely think about the shop while we are throwing something away. Repair, in that sense, is not just a practical skill but a way of reconnecting those two ends. Seeing the two ends of that journey together — that is the bigger picture this unit is named after, and it is one we hope readers will not forget the next time they reach for the bin.

activities.title: Language focus 1 — relative clauses: defining, non-defining and reduced

data.title: Relative clauses: defining, non-defining and reduced
data.can: I can use defining and non-defining relative clauses accurately, including the commas, and reduce a clause with a participle.
data.intro: Liam's article contains several relative clauses that add information smoothly, without starting a new sentence: a small repair workshop, whose owner spends her days…, the trades we have been studying…, gases that warm the planet. Some clauses identify exactly which noun we mean (defining); others simply add extra information about something already identified (non-defining), and some drop the relative pronoun altogether (reduced).

examples.text: The man who repaired my bike works near the school.
examples.note: defining — no commas; identifies which man

examples.text: My bike, which is nearly ten years old, still works perfectly.
The workshop whose owner we interviewed is near school.
examples.note: whose = possessive, for people or things

examples.text: The tools used by carpenters are often passed down for generations.
Sofía, who led the research, found the workshop.
The rubbish that cannot be recycled ends up in landfill.
Objects thrown away too soon often end up harming the environment.

rules: Defining clauses identify exactly which person or thing we mean. Use who / which / that with NO commas.
Non-defining clauses add extra information about something already identified. Use commas on both sides, and never use that.
Use whose for possession, for both people and things: the man whose car…, the company whose products…
You can reduce a clause by dropping the relative pronoun and the auxiliary be: the tools (which are) used by carpenters.
In defining clauses, you can also drop who / which / that when it is the object of the clause: the workshop (that) we visited.
Commas change the meaning: My brother who lives in Lima is a carpenter (I have more than one brother) vs My brother, who lives in Lima, is a carpenter (I have only one brother).

items.sentence: The tools ___ carpenters use are often expensive.
Nadia, ___ idea impressed everyone, spoke first.
This is the article ___ we read for homework.
My uncle, ___ repairs furniture for a living, taught me a lot.
The rubbish ___ in landfill sites can take decades to break down.
The workshop, ___ is run by two brothers, is always busy.

activities.title: Reading and Use of English Part 2 — open cloze. Write ONE word in each gap.

tips.expect: A short text with eight gaps. You write one word in each gap — no options are given. The missing words are mostly grammar words: articles, prepositions, pronouns, relative words, linkers, or parts of a fixed phrase.
how: Read the whole text first: the sentence around a gap often decides the answer.
Look at both sides of the gap: does it need a preposition after a verb, a relative pronoun, or a word to complete a phrase like 'as well as'?
Only one word fits each gap, and contractions are not allowed.
tips.remember: Check your spelling. A correct word spelt wrongly scores nothing.

data.text: Recycling has become part of daily life in many schools, yet the results vary enormously from one building to the next. Most schools now have some kind of recycling scheme, but not all of them work {1} well as they should. A bin that is never emptied is {2} no use to anyone, and pupils quickly lose interest {3} sorting rubbish if nothing seems to change. The schools {4} schemes work best are usually the ones {5} give pupils a clear reason to take part — a competition between classes, for example, {6} a visible result, such as a garden built {7} recycled materials. It is not enough {8} put a sign above a bin and hope for the best; people need to see that their small effort leads somewhere, and that somebody is actually checking what happens to the rubbish afterwards. Once pupils notice a real difference, the habit tends to stick, and the scheme keeps running long after the novelty has worn off.

activities.title: Listening Part 3 — multiple matching. Match each speaker with what they do for the environment.

tips.expect: Five short monologues, about 30 seconds each, on a related topic. For each speaker (1–5) you choose one of eight options (A–H) that best matches what they say. Three options are not needed. You hear the recordings twice.
how: Read all eight options before you listen, and think about how each idea might be paraphrased.
The answer is rarely the exact word you hear — the options rewrite the idea in different words.
Do not choose an option just because you recognise one word from it; check that it matches the whole idea.
tips.remember: Three options are never used. If two options seem to fit one speaker, wait — one of them almost certainly belongs to somebody else.

data.voice_note: Five speakers (Speaker 1 to Speaker 5) talk in turn about what they personally do to help the environment.
data.script:
Speaker 1: At home, we've started separating our food waste from everything else. Peelings, eggshells, old bread — all of that used to go straight in with the rest of the rubbish, but now it goes into a special bin in the garden instead. After a few months it turns into this dark, crumbly material that's brilliant for the plants. It sounds like a small thing, but our black bin is barely half full by the time it gets collected now, which says a lot about how much of what we throw away isn't really rubbish at all. [pause]
Speaker 2: My parents used to drop me off outside school every morning, engine running in a queue of cars for a good ten minutes. Last year I asked if I could travel in some other way instead, and honestly it's the best change I've made. It takes about the same amount of time once you count the traffic, I get some exercise before lessons even start, and there's no petrol involved at all. The only difficulty is when it's raining, but even then I'd rather arrive a bit wet than add to that queue outside the gate every day. [pause]
Speaker 3: I used to buy new clothes almost every month, mostly things I only wore a couple of times before losing interest. A friend persuaded me to try a shop that sells things other people no longer want, and I was amazed by what was there — some items still had the original tags on. Now it's genuinely my first choice rather than something I do occasionally to save money, and my wardrobe is actually more interesting for it. [pause]
Speaker 4: We turned a corner of the garden that used to be completely wasted space into a few raised beds, and we now grow tomatoes, lettuce and herbs through most of the year. It isn't enough to replace a weekly shop, not even close, but there's something satisfying about eating a salad you planted yourself, with none of the packaging that normally comes with it. My grandmother thinks it's funny that we're excited about something she did her whole life without thinking twice. [pause]
Speaker 5: A few months ago a friend invited me to help clear rubbish from the river near our neighbourhood, and I've been going back most weekends since. We usually collect several bags of plastic bottles, wrappers and other bits people have dropped or left behind. It's not glamorous work, and some mornings the amount of rubbish is honestly a bit depressing, but the difference afterwards is obvious, and a couple of passers-by have even come back the following week to join in properly.

activities.title: Language focus 2 — quantifiers and countable/uncountable nouns

data.title: Quantifiers: much, many, a great deal of, few, little, plenty of
data.can: I can choose the right quantifier for countable and uncountable nouns when talking about waste, energy and resources.
data.intro: Talking about the environment means talking about amounts — how much waste we produce, how many resources we use. Words like waste, energy and research are uncountable in English, even though it can feel natural to imagine a plural.

examples.text: We don't produce much waste at home these days.
How many plastic bottles do you use in a week?
There has been a great deal of research into renewable energy.
examples.note: a great deal of + uncountable, formal

examples.text: There is little energy to spare if everyone leaves the lights on.
There are plenty of ways to reduce your own waste.
examples.note: plenty of + countable or uncountable, positive

examples.text: A few small changes make a big difference.
examples.note: a few (some) is positive, unlike few (almost none)

rules: Waste, energy, research, rubbish, information and equipment are uncountable in English: they have no plural and take much / little / a great deal of, never many / few + -s.
Many, few and a few go with countable plural nouns (bottles, changes, people); much, little and a great deal of go with uncountable nouns (energy, waste, research).
Plenty of and a lot of work with BOTH countable and uncountable nouns.
Few and little (without 'a') sound negative, meaning almost none. A few and a little sound positive, meaning some or enough.
In formal writing, a great deal of or a large amount of sound more natural than much, which is more common in questions and negatives (I don't have much time).

items.sentence: There isn't ___ point in recycling just one bottle a week.
How ___ plastic bags does your family use every month?
___ research has been done on ocean plastic in the last decade.
___ people realise how much water is wasted every day.
We have ___ time before the recycling truck arrives — let's hurry.
There are ___ small things you can do today to help.

activities.title: Reading and Use of English Part 3 — word formation. Use the word in capitals to form a word that fits each gap.

tips.expect: A short text with eight gaps. Beside each gap is a word in capitals; you must change its form — a noun, an adjective, an adverb, a negative, a plural — so that it fits the meaning and the grammar of the sentence.
how: Decide first what part of speech is missing: a noun, an adjective, an adverb, a plural?
Check the words before and after the gap — an article or adjective often signals a noun; an -ly ending often signals an adverb.
Watch for negative prefixes (un-, in-, dis-) and for irregular spelling changes, such as responsible → responsibility.
tips.remember: The base word almost always has to change; using it unchanged is never the right answer.

data.text: Anyone walking along a beach today is likely to notice how much plastic waste washes up with the tide. Plastic {1:POLLUTE} is one of the most visible signs of our throwaway culture. Every year, millions of tonnes of packaging end up in rivers and oceans, most of it far from {2:BIODEGRADE}. Scientists warn that without a serious {3:REDUCE} in how much plastic we produce, the problem will only get worse. Public {4:AWARE} of the issue has grown enormously in the last ten years, partly thanks to documentaries showing the effect on wildlife. Even so, {5:ENVIRONMENT} groups argue that awareness alone is not enough: real change depends on {6:CONSUME} habits actually shifting, not just on people feeling guilty. Governments, too, have a {7:RESPONSIBLE} to make recycling easier and cheaper than throwing things away. The good news is that more schools, shops and local councils are {8:INCREASE} choosing reusable materials over single-use plastic, which suggests that the bigger picture may finally be starting to change.

activities.title: Writing Part 2 — report. Plan, write 140–190 words and hand it in.

tips.expect: Part 2 offers a choice of task, and a report is one of the options that can appear. You are usually asked to describe a situation and make a recommendation, for a named reader such as a head teacher or a class. Reports use clear, factual language and often have section headings. 140–190 words.
how: Use two, three or four short section headings in bold, so the reader can find information quickly.
Keep the style factual and fairly formal: avoid contractions and personal storytelling.
Base every section on the task: what you are describing, one clear problem, and one specific recommendation.
tips.remember: A report is marked down if it reads like an informal letter. Headings, short paragraphs and a clear recommendation matter more than colourful language.

data.task:
Your school council has asked you to write a report about recycling at your school, to be read by the head teacher.

Include information about:

  • how well recycling currently works at school
  • one problem you have noticed
  • a recommendation for improvement

Write your report in 140–190 words in an appropriate style, using clear section headings.
plan: Introduction (one sentence): state the purpose of the report.
Current situation: describe briefly how recycling works now.
The problem: describe ONE clear problem you have noticed, with a short example.
Recommendation: one specific, realistic suggestion, and why it would help.

Introducing the report: The purpose of this report is to…
This report looks at…, with a view to…
Describing the situation: On the whole, the scheme works reasonably well, although…
Introducing a problem: However, one issue that needs addressing is…
Recommending: It would therefore be advisable to…
One simple solution would be to…

checklist: I have used clear section headings, in bold.
My report includes the current situation, one problem and one recommendation.
I have used a formal, impersonal style, with no contractions.
I have used at least two relative clauses to add information.
I have used quantifiers correctly (a great deal of waste, few pupils, and so on).
data.model:
A model answer (161 words). Notice the four section headings and the single, clear recommendation.

Introduction

The purpose of this report is to look at how recycling currently works at our school and to recommend one change that could make it more effective.

Current situation

Most classrooms have a blue bin for paper, and pupils generally use it without being reminded. The canteen also separates plastic bottles, which are collected twice a week, so recycling already forms part of the daily routine for most pupils.

The problem

However, food waste from lunchtime is still thrown into the general bin, even though a great deal of it could be composted instead. Few pupils seem aware that this option even exists, and there is currently no bin for it anywhere near the tables.

Recommendation

I would therefore recommend introducing a clearly labelled compost bin in the canteen, along with a short assembly explaining what can go in it. This would reduce general waste significantly and, in time, cost very little to set up compared with current waste-collection fees.

activities.title: Speaking — Parts 3 and 4. Collaborative task and discussion. Record your best answer.

tips.expect: Part 3 (about 4 minutes): you and your partner talk together about five written ideas for about 2 minutes, then have about a minute to reach a decision together. Part 4 (about 4 minutes): the examiner asks you both further questions on the same topic.
how: In Part 3 you are not marked on agreeing; you are marked on interacting — ask your partner's opinion, respond to it, and build on it.
Do not try to cover all five ideas in detail. Three in depth is better than five in a rush.
In the decision minute, negotiate: Shall we say…? I'd agree with that, as long as…
In Part 4, develop your answers: opinion → reason → example.
tips.remember: Look at your partner, not at the examiner, during Part 3. The examiner is listening, not talking.

data.text: Part 3: discuss how much difference each of these actions makes to the environment, then decide together which makes the biggest difference. Part 4: discuss consumption, waste and personal responsibility.
